items.question_text: A term baby is born at 3 am in a Melbourne public hospital. The mother is hepatitis B surface-antigen negative, and the antenatal record is complete. Birth weight is 3400 g. The baby is well, breastfeeding, and has no risk factors for perinatal transmission. The night registrar is about to leave the ward and suggests leaving the birth dose of hepatitis B until the 6-week GP check, because the mother is negative and the baby looks well. The parents are happy to vaccinate and ask if delaying is safer. The midwife has the vaccine drawn up. There is no contraindication. Birth hepatitis B is given as soon as practicable, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 7 days, regardless of maternal status. Waiting for the 6-week check is the error. What is the most appropriate advice?  The antenatal serology is on the file and was repeated in the third trimester. There is no maternal risk behaviour that would change the plan. The baby has had vitamin K. The parents have no objection. Delaying to 6 weeks leaves a window the birth dose is designed to close. The dose should be given now, before the registrar leaves.  Observation for the usual post-vaccine period is planned. There is no family history of vaccine reaction. The 6-week check remains for the other infant vaccines. It is not a substitute for the birth dose of hepatitis B.  The parents ask if a negative mother means the baby cannot catch hepatitis B later. Explain that the birth dose is population protection, not only perinatal. Give it now.
options: Give the birth dose of hepatitis B now
Omit the birth dose because maternal surface antigen is negative
Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin instead of vaccine
Defer the dose until the 6-week check so it can be combined
Test the baby for surface antibody before any vaccine
items.subtopic: Birth hepatitis B is given as soon as practicable, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 7 days.
items.explanation:
Every infant is offered a birth dose of hepatitis B, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 7 days. Maternal surface-antigen negativity does not remove the birth dose. Immunoglobulin is added for babies of infectious mothers. It does not replace vaccine in this baby.

A. Give the birth dose of hepatitis B now
The baby is inside the window, the parents consent, and the program dose is due.

B. Omit the birth dose because maternal surface antigen is negative
Negative maternal antigen changes the need for immunoglobulin, not the universal birth dose.

C. Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin instead of vaccine
Immunoglobulin is for babies of infectious mothers, with vaccine, not instead of it.

D. Defer the dose until the 6-week check so it can be combined
Six weeks is outside the birth-dose window.

E. Test the baby for surface antibody before any vaccine
A well term baby does not need serology before the birth dose.
items.diagnosis_explanation: A well term baby of a surface-antigen-negative mother still receives the birth dose of hepatitis B now, not at 6 weeks.
key_takeaways: Birth hepatitis B is universal, ideally within 24 hours and by 7 days.
Negative maternal antigen removes immunoglobulin, not the vaccine.

items.question_text: A 16-week-old infant in Adelaide is brought for vaccines that were missed after a move interstate. He is well, afebrile, and has had no intussusception. He has never had a rotavirus dose. The first dose of Rotarix cannot be started once the infant has turned 15 weeks. He is now 16 weeks. A locum suggests giving it anyway because the child is behind and the family are keen. The other infant vaccines that are due can still be given. Rotavirus is the one with the hard age limit on the first dose. Starting it now is outside the schedule. What is the most appropriate advice about rotavirus?  He is growing well and has no chronic gastrointestinal disease. The family moved at 10 weeks and missed the 4-month visit. Other due vaccines, including the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis and pneumococcal doses, can proceed. Only rotavirus has this upper age limit on the first dose. Explaining that clearly avoids a dose given outside the schedule.  The AIR confirms no rotavirus dose ever. He is past the 14-week and 6-day limit for the first Rotarix dose. Document the missed window so a later clinician does not try to start it. Continue the rest of the catch-up.  Write the age limit in the notes. The family are anxious about being behind. Reassure them the other vaccines proceed. Rotavirus does not.
options: Give the first rotavirus dose today and book the second in 8 weeks
Do not start rotavirus. The first Rotarix dose cannot be given once the infant has turned 15 weeks
Give rotavirus only if a stool viral PCR is negative
Replace rotavirus with an extra pneumococcal dose
Give both rotavirus doses today to finish the course
items.subtopic: The first Rotarix dose cannot be started once the infant has turned 15 weeks.
items.explanation:
On the NIP the rotavirus product is Rotarix. The first dose must be given by 14 weeks, before the infant turns 15 weeks, and the second by 24 weeks. At 16 weeks he cannot start the course. The rest of the overdue infant schedule can still be planned. A negative stool test does not reopen the age window.

A. Give the first rotavirus dose today and book the second in 8 weeks
The catch-up instinct is the trap. The upper age has already passed.

B. Do not start rotavirus. The first Rotarix dose cannot be given once the infant has turned 15 weeks
This is the age rule. Continue the other overdue vaccines.

C. Give rotavirus only if a stool viral PCR is negative
Viral clearance does not change the age limit.

D. Replace rotavirus with an extra pneumococcal dose
Pneumococcal has its own schedule. It is not a substitute dose.

E. Give both rotavirus doses today to finish the course
Two doses on one day are not a catch-up, and he is already too old to start.
items.diagnosis_explanation: At 16 weeks the first Rotarix dose is too late. Catch-up does not override that age limit.
key_takeaways: First Rotarix dose by 14 weeks, before turning 15 weeks. Second by 24 weeks.
Other overdue infant vaccines are not cancelled by this rule.

items.question_text: A woman in Perth is 24 weeks pregnant in her second pregnancy. She received dTpa at 28 weeks in the last pregnancy, three years ago. She asks if she needs it again or if the previous dose covers this baby. She is well, with no contraindication to the vaccine. Pertussis vaccine is recommended at 20 to 32 weeks in each pregnancy, to protect the newborn. A dose in a previous pregnancy does not cover this one. She is inside the window now. What is the most appropriate advice?  She had no reaction to the previous dTpa. This pregnancy is uncomplicated. She is not near delivery. The point of the dose is transplacental antibody for the newborn, so it is repeated each pregnancy in the recommended window. A dose three years ago does not provide that for this baby. She should have it now.  Antibody from a dose years ago will have waned for the purpose of protecting this newborn. The recommendation is explicit: each pregnancy, 20 to 32 weeks. She is at 24 weeks. Give dTpa now.  She can have it in the antenatal clinic or at the GP. Either is fine. The error is skipping it because of a dose in the last pregnancy.
options: Skip dTpa because the last dose was within 10 years
Give dTpa only if a contact has pertussis
Give dTpa now, in this pregnancy
Defer dTpa until 37 weeks so the antibodies are fresher
Give a childhood DTPa formulation instead
items.subtopic: Pertussis vaccine is recommended at 20 to 32 weeks in each pregnancy.
items.explanation:
A single dTpa dose is recommended in every pregnancy, preferably between 20 and 32 weeks, to protect the newborn. A dose 3 years ago does not cover this baby. Thirty-seven weeks is later than the preferred window.

A. Skip dTpa because the last dose was within 10 years
The adult booster interval is not the pregnancy rule.

B. Give dTpa only if a contact has pertussis
Pregnancy vaccination is routine, not outbreak-only.

C. Give dTpa now, in this pregnancy
She is inside 20 to 32 weeks, and each pregnancy needs its own dose.

D. Defer dTpa until 37 weeks so the antibodies are fresher
The preferred window is 20 to 32 weeks.

E. Give a childhood DTPa formulation instead
The pregnancy product is the adult dTpa formulation.
items.diagnosis_explanation: At 24 weeks she should have dTpa in this pregnancy. A dose 3 years ago does not protect this newborn.
key_takeaways: Pregnancy dTpa is once each pregnancy, preferably 20 to 32 weeks.
The 10-year adult interval does not apply here.

items.question_text: A woman in Hobart is 8 weeks pregnant and asks for the influenza vaccine because her toddler is in childcare. A receptionist has told her to wait until the second trimester. She is well, with no egg anaphylaxis and no previous reaction to the vaccine. Influenza vaccine is inactivated and can be given at any stage of pregnancy, in every pregnancy. Waiting for the second trimester is unnecessary. What is the most appropriate advice?  She has no febrile illness today. The toddler's childcare has had several respiratory infections. Influenza in pregnancy protects her and the newborn. The inactivated vaccine has no trimester restriction. The receptionist's advice to wait is the old habit, not the current recommendation. She can be vaccinated today.  No live vaccine is being considered. Influenza is inactivated. First-trimester administration is acceptable and recommended when the vaccine is available. Do not defer to 13 weeks.  Childcare exposure is a reason to give it, not to delay. Any trimester is acceptable. Vaccinate today.  She has no contraindication. The toddler's childcare is the exposure that prompted the visit. That supports giving the vaccine, not delaying it. Any stage of pregnancy is acceptable for inactivated influenza vaccine.
options: Wait until 28 weeks, with the pertussis vaccine
Influenza vaccine is contraindicated before 12 weeks
Give live attenuated influenza vaccine today
Give inactivated influenza vaccine now
Test for influenza IgG and vaccinate only if negative
items.subtopic: Influenza vaccine can be given at any stage of pregnancy, in every pregnancy.
items.explanation:
Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended at any stage of each pregnancy. Waiting for the third trimester leaves her uncovered through the first half of pregnancy. Live attenuated influenza vaccine is not the pregnancy product.

A. Wait until 28 weeks, with the pertussis vaccine
Pertussis has a preferred window. Influenza does not need to wait for it.

B. Influenza vaccine is contraindicated before 12 weeks
There is no first-trimester ban on inactivated influenza vaccine.

C. Give live attenuated influenza vaccine today
Live influenza vaccine is not used in pregnancy.

D. Give inactivated influenza vaccine now
Any stage, this pregnancy, no contraindication.

E. Test for influenza IgG and vaccinate only if negative
Serology does not decide seasonal influenza vaccination.
items.diagnosis_explanation: At 8 weeks she can have inactivated influenza vaccine now. It is not held until the third trimester.
key_takeaways: Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended at any stage of every pregnancy.
Do not apply the pertussis window to influenza.

items.question_text: A woman in Cairns is 10 weeks pregnant. Her serology shows she is not immune to rubella. She is travelling to a region with a measles outbreak in six weeks and asks for MMR now so she is covered before she goes. MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It can be planned after delivery. Giving it now is the error. What is the most appropriate advice?  Rubella non-immunity is noted. MMR would address that, but not in pregnancy. Travel advice and post-exposure planning can be discussed. The vaccine itself waits until after delivery, when she is no longer pregnant. Giving a live vaccine now is contraindicated.  Postnatal MMR can be arranged before she leaves hospital or at the 6-week check, once pregnancy is over. Travel precautions are separate. The injection today is not MMR.  Document non-immunity and the plan for postnatal MMR. Do not give the live vaccine this trimester, whatever the travel date.  Travel in six weeks does not override the live-vaccine contraindication. Measles protection for a pregnant woman who is susceptible is a public-health and exposure question, not a reason to inject MMR today.
options: Give MMR today and repeat it after 4 weeks
Give MMR if a dating scan is normal
Give varicella vaccine instead, because it is safer in pregnancy
Delay travel advice and give MMR in the second trimester
Do not give MMR in pregnancy. Plan it after delivery
items.subtopic: MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
items.explanation:
MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. Non-immune status and travel do not override that. Varicella vaccine is also live and also contraindicated. She can be vaccinated after delivery, and pregnancy should be avoided for 28 days after MMR.

A. Give MMR today and repeat it after 4 weeks
Two doses do not make a live vaccine safe in pregnancy.

B. Give MMR if a dating scan is normal
A normal scan does not clear a live vaccine.

C. Give varicella vaccine instead, because it is safer in pregnancy
Varicella vaccine is also live and contraindicated.

D. Delay travel advice and give MMR in the second trimester
The contraindication is pregnancy, not the first trimester alone.

E. Do not give MMR in pregnancy. Plan it after delivery
This is the handbook rule. Discuss travel risk separately.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Non-immune rubella serology in a pregnant woman is a reason to plan MMR after delivery, not to give it now.
key_takeaways: Live vaccines, including MMR and varicella, are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Avoid pregnancy for 28 days after MMR.

items.question_text: A 45-year-old man with a history of egg anaphylaxis, which required adrenaline, asks for the influenza vaccine. He is well today. A colleague says egg allergy is a contraindication and he should be referred to hospital for any dose. Egg anaphylaxis is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination in a setting that can treat anaphylaxis. He can be vaccinated here today. What is the most appropriate advice?  His egg anaphylaxis was five years ago and is well documented. He has no anaphylaxis to a previous influenza vaccine. The clinic has adrenaline and a place to observe him. Egg allergy, including anaphylaxis, is not a reason to withhold influenza vaccine in that setting. Hospital referral is not required for this indication.  Observe him for the recommended period after the dose. Adrenaline is available. That is the setting the advice assumes. Withholding the vaccine for egg anaphylaxis is outdated.  He has asked specifically about egg. The answer is that he can be vaccinated here. Do not send him away for that history.
options: Give inactivated influenza vaccine here today
Influenza vaccine is absolutely contraindicated after egg anaphylaxis
Skin-test him with raw egg white before any dose
Give the vaccine only after a graded egg challenge
Use half the dose and observe him at home
items.subtopic: Egg anaphylaxis is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination in a setting that can treat anaphylaxis.
items.explanation:
Anaphylaxis to egg is not a contraindication to inactivated influenza vaccine. He can be vaccinated in a setting that can manage anaphylaxis. Skin testing and egg challenge are not the pathway, and a half dose is not a recommendation.

A. Give inactivated influenza vaccine here today
The clinic can treat anaphylaxis, and egg anaphylaxis does not bar the dose.

B. Influenza vaccine is absolutely contraindicated after egg anaphylaxis
That pharmacy rule is outdated.

C. Skin-test him with raw egg white before any dose
Egg skin testing does not decide influenza vaccination.

D. Give the vaccine only after a graded egg challenge
He does not need to pass an egg challenge first.

E. Use half the dose and observe him at home
A reduced dose at home is not the alternative.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Egg anaphylaxis does not stop inactivated influenza vaccine when the clinic can treat anaphylaxis.
key_takeaways: Egg allergy, including anaphylaxis, is not a flu-vaccine contraindication.
Vaccinate where anaphylaxis can be treated. Do not skin-test first.

items.question_text: A 4-year-old had anaphylaxis, with wheeze and collapse, within minutes of a previous dose of a vaccine. The parent asks for the same vaccine today because the child is due a booster. Anaphylaxis after a previous dose of that vaccine is a contraindication to further doses of it. A mild local reaction would be different. This is not mild. The vaccine should not be given. What is the most appropriate advice?  The previous reaction was within 15 minutes, with respiratory and circulatory features, and adrenaline was given. That is anaphylaxis to that vaccine. A later-dose local redness would not be a contraindication. This history is. The booster of that vaccine is not given. An alternative schedule can be discussed.  Record the anaphylaxis clearly so it is not repeated at the next visit. Other vaccines that he has tolerated can continue. This one stops.  Parents sometimes confuse a fever after a vaccine with anaphylaxis. This history is anaphylaxis. Withhold this vaccine.  Collapse and wheeze with adrenaline is anaphylaxis. It is recorded against this vaccine. Further doses of it are contraindicated. Do not proceed because a booster is due.
options: Give a different brand of the same vaccine today
Do not give this vaccine. Anaphylaxis after a previous dose is a contraindication
Give half the dose and keep him for 4 hours
Premedicate with an oral antihistamine and vaccinate
Record a conscientious objection instead of a medical contraindication
items.subtopic: Anaphylaxis after a previous dose is a contraindication to that vaccine.
items.explanation:
Anaphylaxis after a previous dose of a vaccine is a contraindication to that vaccine. A brand change, a half dose, or an antihistamine does not remove it. This is a medical contraindication, not a conscientious objection, and it should be confirmed and recorded by an approved practitioner.

A. Give a different brand of the same vaccine today
The reaction was to the vaccine, not a reason to swap brands and proceed.

B. Do not give this vaccine. Anaphylaxis after a previous dose is a contraindication
This is the handbook stop rule.

C. Give half the dose and keep him for 4 hours
Dose-splitting is not how anaphylaxis is managed.

D. Premedicate with an oral antihistamine and vaccinate
Antihistamine does not make a contraindicated dose safe.

E. Record a conscientious objection instead of a medical contraindication
The parents are not objecting. The child had anaphylaxis.
items.diagnosis_explanation: Anaphylaxis after the 18-month dose means do not give that vaccine today, including under another brand.
key_takeaways: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose contraindicates the same vaccine.
This is a medical contraindication, not an objection.

items.question_text: A 12-month-old is due for vaccines and has a clear runny nose and a temperature of 37.6°C. He is feeding well and is not toxic. A grandparent says any illness means the vaccines should be deferred for two weeks. A mild afebrile or low-grade illness is not a reason to defer a due vaccine. He can be vaccinated today. What is the most appropriate advice?  He has been like this for a day. There is no wheeze, no rash, and no dehydration. Deferring for a minor illness delays protection and often leads to further missed visits. The due vaccines can be given. The grandparent's two-week rule is not the schedule rule.  If he were febrile and toxic, or had a serious evolving illness, deferral would be reasonable. A runny nose and 37.6°C is not that. Vaccinate today and advise on common reactions.  Give the 12-month vaccines. Advise on fever and the usual local reaction. Do not rebook for a cold.  Feeding well and not toxic is the picture of a minor illness. Due vaccines are given. A two-week deferral for a cold is not indicated.
options: Defer all vaccines until he has been well for 2 weeks
Give antibiotics for 3 days and vaccinate after the course
Give the due vaccines today
Give MMR only and postpone the others until the coryza settles
Swap MMR for immunoglobulin because he is mildly unwell
items.subtopic: A mild afebrile illness is not a reason to defer a due vaccine.
items.explanation:
A mild illness without significant fever is not a contraindication. He is due the due 12-month vaccines and is well enough to have them. Waiting 2 weeks, or splitting off MMR, is unnecessary. Immunoglobulin is not the substitute for a well catch-up.

A. Defer all vaccines until he has been well for 2 weeks
The grandmother's rule creates a missed visit.

B. Give antibiotics for 3 days and vaccinate after the course
There is no indication for antibiotics, and they are not a vaccine prelude.

C. Give the due vaccines today
Mild coryza, normal feeding, and 37.2°C do not defer the 12-month set.

D. Give MMR only and postpone the others until the coryza settles
The same mild illness does not pick off three of the the due 12-month vaccines.

E. Swap MMR for immunoglobulin because he is mildly unwell
He needs vaccine, not replacement immunoglobulin.
items.diagnosis_explanation: A smiling, feeding 12-month-old with a runny nose and 37.2°C can have his due vaccines today.
key_takeaways: Mild illness without significant fever is not a contraindication.
Do not split a due visit because of coryza.

items.diagnosis_explanation: At 24, with no risk condition, she can catch up a single HPV dose. She has not aged out at the end of school.
key_takeaways: HPV catch-up runs to 26 years.
